entries.title: Everything Apple Announced: iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch, AirPods 5
entries.summary: The company’s September event introduced Apple’s first ever foldable iPhone, along with new iPhone 18 Pro models, updates to the Apple Watch, some AirPods, and more advances to Siri AI.
entries.content:
It’s a brand new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.

At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.

The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.

As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.

Here’s everything Apple showed off today.

Apple iPhone Duo

Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.

It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.

The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.

The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhones 18) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.

On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.

Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.

Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.

Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.

For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.

iPhone 18 Pro

As predictions suspected, Apple is not releasing its base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.

They come with Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.

The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.

The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.

Adjustable Aperture

The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.

Apple is also touting improved photography and video capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.

Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.

The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.

Apple Watch

Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.

The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.

Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.

These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.

The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.

There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.

For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.

AirPods 5

Apple’s new, cheaper AirPods 5 come with some of the features that the AirPods 4 had. The AirPods 5 come with noise canceling and adaptive sound controls. You can also use Siri AI directly on the AirPods and communicate via chat. They also have live language translation, though it’s not clear how well that will function out in the real world—of course, it works great in Apple’s demo videos.

The base model costs $129. There’s also a version with touch volume controls on the stems, a little more battery, and a wireless case-charging puck that also can charge your Apple Watch. Those nicer options cost $149.

Some rumors had predicted that Apple would show off a new pair of AirPods with cameras in the earbuds. Those are possibly still coming eventually, but Apple didn't say anything about them this time. We’re expecting at least one more Apple event before the end of the year, and they may show up then.

entries.title: Apple Doesn’t Want You to Worry About the New Apple Watch’s Listening Features
entries.summary: The new Apple Watch includes several “intelligent” listening features that have privacy and security baked in. But the protections can’t change the facts of what the tools do.
entries.content:
The new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come not just with better fitness tracking and upgraded noise reduction, but also a whole new way to listen.

Apple announced on Wednesday that the two smartwatches come with four opt-in “audio intelligence” tools that are powered by audio gathered by the watches’ microphones. They include sound and music recognition, a conversation recap feature, and “Live Rewind” so a user can see a transcription of anything that was said in their environment in the previous 15 seconds.

Seemingly wary that the features could make it feel like the walls have ears, Apple is emphasizing that all of them are built to prioritize privacy and security using the extensive infrastructure the company has developed to protect its other Apple Intelligence and Siri services. As more and more of these types of features debut, though, the audio intelligence announcements are a reminder that AI-powered tools are becoming increasingly universal in all areas of computing and life.

“These features do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple,” the company wrote in a report shared with WIRED.

The new Apple Watch features are designed to process as much data locally on devices as possible, so potentially sensitive data doesn’t go to the cloud. Sound Recognition, for example, alerts users about sounds in their environment—including doorbells, sirens, alarms, or, say, a baby crying—without sending any data off the watch. The tools that do send information out to the cloud preprocess the data so it isn’t raw audio files, then use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.

Apple emphasizes that its on-device capabilities for Apple watches have expanded thanks to the company’s new S11 chips. The chips include a special memory-protected space that Apple calls the Secure Exclave. Designed specifically for sensor data, the exclave is an isolated buffer that is inaccessible to the rest of the operating system where Apple Watch can hold and process audio data in a protected space.

A new Shazam feature “listens” for music and will generate a signature of a song that is stored in the Secure Exclave. If the user navigates to Shazam to find out what the music is, the tool will send that signature—not an audio file—to Shazam’s servers for identification. (Shazam is an Apple-owned service.) If the user doesn’t prompt to identify the music, or as soon as they do, the special signature is “immediately” deleted from the watch.

The recap feature, known as Siri Recap, can be set to be on all the time and generate recaps of any substantive conversation, or it can be given a schedule to listen in at certain times during the day. A dedicated AI model determines when speech is occurring without recording or transcribing any data. If it detects a conversation, audio goes into a protected buffer within the Secure Exclave on the Apple Watch, the watch encrypts it, and then transmits it using Apple’s special secure Bluetooth pairing to the Secure Exclave on a user’s iPhone. Then the audio is immediately deleted from the Apple Watch.

The iPhone uses local speech recognition and language models on-device to transcribe the audio and then generate a minimal version of the transcript that removes nonessential elements like extra words and repeated phrases. Then the raw audio is immediately deleted from the iPhone as well. The last step on the iPhone is a safety model that “screens the text to omit potentially harmful terms,” according to Apple. From there, the distillation of the conversation is encrypted, and the iPhone sends it out to Private Cloud Compute.

“Contextual information is also sent to improve summary quality,” Apple says. “For example, Now Playing data helps the model understand that speech may have originated from music or a podcast. Calendar data can help generate accurate titles of summaries. High-level location labels such as home, work, and school, along with locality information such as city, state, and country, add context to the summarization. Point-of-interest categories like ‘grocery store’ or ‘park’ may also be included. Precise location and specific points of interest are not included.”

Finally, the condensed transcript is run through Apple’s foundation models in Private Cloud Compute to create a title and summary, which is then encrypted and sent back to the iPhone and Apple Watch. Apple says that Siri Recap is built to remove sensitive information like financial data, ID numbers, or other personal identifiers from its summaries.

The Live Rewind features that lets users ask for a text version of the last 15 seconds of what was said in their environment uses the Secure Exclave buffer to continuously hold audio on a rolling basis, where old sound is replaced by new audio and doesn’t amass. To get a transcript through Live Rewind, users must double-press the Apple Watch’s Digital Crown each time. Once activated, the watch sends the last 15 seconds of buffered audio from its Secure Exclave to the Secure Exclave of the paired iPhone. If the iPhone is not available, the transfer will fail, and the audio will automatically be deleted. (Siri Recap has similar fail-safes if the transfer from the watch to the iPhone fails.) If the transfer goes through, the iPhone does on-device speech-recognition processing to make a transcript and then deletes the audio and sends the text back to the Apple Watch. Users read the transcript and then can discard it or save it in the Siri app.

It's hard to ignore that, in spite of all of these data protections, anyone wearing a new Apple Watch could be siccing “audio intelligence” on, say, your intimate vent session, private family update, or accidental slip-up about a secret. To try to mitigate blatant privacy violations, Apple says that the watch produces an audible chime when a watch owner initiates a Live Rewind transcript to alert other people in the area—even if it is on silent mode or paired with headphones. And the features are built to omit or filter out potentially identifying information about speakers. But the sheer scope and breadth of the tools is extremely noteworthy.

Apple has invested significantly over many years in its secure AI processing infrastructure—far beyond what almost any other company has done. The new audio features highlight, though, that over time the AI attack surface, or sheer quantity of services and systems that could include flaws or mistakes and be attacked, is growing faster than the implications can be fully understood.

entries.title: UK Lawmakers Are Freaking Out Over AI’s Summer of Chaos
entries.summary: As AI agents go rogue and fears of superintelligence grow, politicians are raising the alarm over its potential harm to human existence.
entries.content:
A leading British politician has urged the United Nations to intervene in “the unsafe development of super intelligence” after an Anthropic team leader posted: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

Whether “marketing hype” or signposting of a genuine extinction threat, “governments must step in,” Labour MP Darren Jones wrote in an open letter also addressed to the UK prime minister and international Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Jones is the latest lawmaker scrambling to find ways to protect the British public from AI threats to safety. Just one day earlier, Labour MP Alex Sobel had introduced a parliamentary bill proposing to ban the “development, deployment, and operation of artificial superintelligence”—systems which can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. The legislation would also give the government powers to monitor and control the development of the technology at different points in the supply chain, including at chip level.

“We are not alone in this effort,” said Sobel while introducing the bill, pointing to the US government’s temporary export ban on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June. "If the Trump Administration, who are perceived as historically against AI regulation, can contemplate drawing a line on models that are too powerful and dangerous, it would be strange for us not to ask what our response should be," he argued.

MPs from across political parties put their names on the bill, including Labour MP Jess Asato, who is suing Elon Musk’s xAI after its Grok chatbot was allegedly used to generate fake sexualized images of her. Lawmakers have become increasingly worried about the threat of AI to national security after a string of incidents of AI agents going rogue in recent months. They want to introduce guardrails against worst-case scenarios, such as these systems seizing control of critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.

The Hugging Face hack by OpenAI’s models that escaped containment in July “is why it’s even more important that we move quickly to regulate and legislate on superintelligent AI,” Sobel tells WIRED, “because AI is developing at pace, and I’m afraid to say those developing it don’t know exactly what’s in it.”

In an unusual move, the parliamentary bill was drafted by the nonprofit ControlAI, which is backed by Skype founding engineer and former DeepMind investor director Jaan Tallinn. He had previously been working at AI safety startup Conjecture but tells WIRED he wanted to make the public and policymakers aware of the “open secret” that “developing superintelligence could cause human extinction.”

Conjecture founder Connor Leahy now leads ControlAI’s US arm, which consulted on Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar’s bill to ban superintelligence development, in addition to having briefed nearly 200 congressional offices and more than 20 members of the Senate and House of Representatives on the extinction risk of superintelligence.

Sobel will present his bill in full in November. While he accepts it’s rare for the UK government to accept private legislation like this, Sobel hopes it may lead the government to work with other countries on an international ban.

Sobel has previously tried in vain to introduce a “kill switch” into the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which would allow the government to pull the plug on any data center hosting an AI agent that presented a threat. The mechanism, which was also proposed by ControlAI, is similar to a law pushed for by both Republican and Democratic lawmakers in the US. AI minister Kanishka Narayan, then working under former prime minister Keir Starmer, shot it down, pointing out that the bill already allows the government powers to intervene if compromised network and information systems cause a national security risk. That could include requiring an entity to cease using and isolate an AI model, he noted.

But that may not be enough, Sobel says, hoping to meet with the government to hammer out details of which companies would be included within the scope of the proposed rules. “I think this might be the crucial year,” he says. “If we leave it too long, things may move past our ability to regulate it.”

Peers across parties in the UK parliament’s upper house, including former AI minister Viscount Camrose, tried unsuccessfully to reintroduce the measure last week. They have been frustrated as the binding regulation on frontier AI firms promised by the Labour government when they won power in 2024 has failed to materialize.

While peer Tim Clement-Jones admitted they shouldn’t be trying to “shoehorn” AI regulation into a cybersecurity bill. In the absence of any other AI legislation, “we have no choice,” he said in a speech to parliament. “We must have more control and oversight over that sort of behavior, because you can see its consequences,” said Alexandra Freeman in the debate, referring to the Hugging Face incident. “This legislation is our only opportunity now.”

Nearly nine out of 10 Britons support independent regulation of the technology, a poll by the Ada Lovelace Institute showed in December. Meanwhile, nearly three times as many (38 percent) believe that the risks of AI outweigh the benefits as vice versa (13 percent), according to official statistics. But “the government has been completely deaf to this, and they have paid no attention to those who are advocating for this,” Clement-Jones says, arguing that the public's lack of trust in the technology will curb adoption.

The UK government evaluates the capabilities and safety of advanced artificial intelligence models through the research body the AI Security Institute. Cooperation is voluntary for AI companies, as the organization has no legal powers to access unreleased models for testing or ban their public release. For example, the agency reportedly did not get access to Anthropic’s latest model, Claude Mythos 5.1, for testing.

“I think it's a rather naive position to imagine that we can do things on a voluntary basis,” says Clement-Jones. “Do you really think that the big AI companies have got everybody's welfare at heart?”

entries.title: I Let an AI Agent Hack All My Gadgets—and I’d Do It Again
entries.summary: After I removed the safety guardrails from a powerful open-source model, it found vulnerabilities in my household devices and hacked into a PC. But it also told me how to make everything a lot more secure.
entries.content:
As the author of a newsletter about artificial intelligence, I consider it my duty to experience the bleeding edge of this technology firsthand. This week, that meant embracing some agentic mayhem.

You’re probably aware that frontier AI models have attained advanced cybersecurity capabilities in recent months. They can find zero-day bugs in large codebases and scan computers for vulnerabilities at lightning speed. To make things even more exciting, cybersecurity agents sometimes go rogue, colluding with one another and hacking into outside systems to gain an edge.

To get a closer look, I decided to unleash one in my own home network. Over the course of a few days, I watched as my own rogue agent found vulnerabilities in various household devices, hacked into a PC, and showed me that several vibe-coded projects were—unsurprisingly—riddled with bugs. (My wife knew what I was up to, and rolled her eyes each time I proudly announced the discovery of a new vulnerability.)

But Will, you might be thinking, giving an impish, all-powerful cybersecurity agent access to your home network is batshit. And you would be correct! Nevertheless, I believe that a good way to understand the cybersecurity hellscape in front of us is to pay it a visit.

In the end, my experiment was revealing, but oddly reassuring, too. My little network gremlin showed me how vulnerable my home life would be to AI hacking, but it also told me how to make everything a lot more secure. In the end, I discovered that the best way to deal with AI hacking may well be having your own AI hacker.

Maverick Model

I got the idea for the experiment after discovering Abliteration AI, a startup that offers access to powerful AI models with the usual guardrails removed.

Most mainstream AI models will refuse to respond to certain queries, and they will certainly refuse to find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. But it’s possible to remove these restrictions by finding and modifying certain patterns within an open-weight model’s internal parameters. You can tweak the patterns that lead to refusals through a process known as abliteration.

Removing AI’s guardrails might seem risky, but it’s not uncommon. Academic researchers use these de-aligned models to better understand how AI actually works, while cybersecurity firms use them to probe software and systems for vulnerabilities. Technically speaking, Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra work similarly: They’re basically conventional models that lack the usual cyber controls, with access limited to trusted customers for the time being. (The companies also offer wider access to models with a medium number of guardrails so that companies can vet their code and systems for problems.)

Abliteration AI offers several fully de-aligned models, the most powerful of which is a version of Z.ai’s latest agentic coding model, GLM 5.3. This puts similar cyber capabilities to Mythos and Astra right in your hands for as little as the cost of a pizza.

Devon, Abliteration AI’s CEO, believes that making de-aligned models widely available is smart defense: It will help good guys counter bad guys by probing systems for vulnerabilities and by mimicking the behavior of hackers, scammers, and, yes, rogue AI agents. (Devon asked that I use his first name only because his day job doesn’t know about his side project.)

“You have all these critical infrastructure companies, from airlines to banks, that are rolling out agents like crazy,” Devon says. “How do you make sure that a nefarious actor can't use some of these agents in a bad way?”

To start, I created an Abliteration AI account and installed a software harness called CyberStrike, which helps guide a large language model through different cybersecurity tasks.

Using CyberStrike, I asked the abliterated version of GLM-5.3 to take a look at my local network. A few moments later, it found around a dozen hardware systems on the same network—and catalogued several vulnerabilities.

My unruly helper told me, for instance, that my printer was misconfigured, which meant that anyone on the network could log into it. That could be a problem if there were sensitive documents—tax returns, bank statements, medical records—in the print queue.

The agent also noted that my Wiim stereo was leaking a lot of information. (It knew that the last song played was Rein Me In by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, if you must know.) Anyone on the network could play what they wanted or adjust the volume. The model also found a bunch of internet-of-things (IoT) devices on the network with firmware that needed updating.

An ungovernable agent could be very useful to a hacker. But mine offered a number of helpful tips for keeping my network secure. Besides updating outdated firmware and securing the printer, it recommended putting IoT devices like smart speakers on a guest network; if one were compromised, it wouldn’t be able to see any of my PCs. Not bad for a model with no morals.

I also asked the agent to take a look at a directory containing a bunch of vibe-coded projects, including some that I turned into simple websites. It found dozens of problems, including unprotected API credentials and a misconfiguration that might let an attacker send out emails. Hardly surprising for a bunch of casually vibe-coded stuff, but still chastening. The sheer number of bugs makes me think I won’t be deploying a line of code without doing some AI vetting first.

Fear Factor

Running an abliterated model is, to put it plainly, a bit scary.

I asked my agent to probe a Linux machine on my network for vulnerabilities. After running a bunch of scans, it reported that the machine seemed relatively secure. I then asked if it could figure out how to log in. It cleverly figured out a working username based on the name of other systems on the network. It tried a bunch of obvious passwords, which didn’t work. It also offered to write a script to try “brute forcing” the password, but I told it to stand down.

To my amazement, the agent then found a cryptographic key on my machine, used it to log in without a password, and started hunting for the password in order to gain root access. I felt a moment of pure panic as I saw it rummaging around the directories. It made me wonder how far the agent might go in order to achieve its goal. Might it have hacked into something else, like a machine outside of my network, in search of the key? Probably not, but who knows with these agents.

Some behavior could prove even more precarious. When I connected to my Wi-Fi network a few hours later and asked the model to see if it could find any new machines, it not only found the router, but decided to try logging in by trying several common “admin/passwords” combinations. If it had decided to do this on an outside network, I could have been in big trouble.

Shaanan Cohney, a computer scientist at Tufts University who specializes in cybersecurity and the law, says that a cyber-reckoning does seem to be coming.

“Attackers are often early adopters,” Cohney says. “There’s also an asymmetry, in that to secure a castle, you need to make sure that there are no holes anywhere or no loose bricks in your wall. To invade a castle, all you need to do is to find that one loose brick.”

Over the long term, Cohney says, the proliferation of cyber-capable models may make software more secure in general. The challenge is that many companies aren’t thinking about shoring up their defenses. “Most organizations have other things to worry about,” he says.

After all that, I shut down the model and went back to using a regular, fully aligned version. Claude Code or Codex will only do certain things related to cybersecurity, like help you configure your laptop’s firewall. But at least they won’t hack your system before you know it. Hopefully.

AI Hacking for All

Unless open-weight models are banned outright, advanced AI hacking capabilities will soon be very widely available. My experiment made me think that this might be just what we need. Assuming that bad guys will have access to AI, shouldn’t we all use it to defend ourselves?

“We need to help people use these capabilities,” says Aleksander Mądry, an MIT professor who studies AI safety and who is currently on leave while he works for OpenAI. “I do think there will be room for open source and independent tools. If only because, ultimately, these kinds of approaches have the real staying power in the world of security.”

Mądry notes, however, that a key issue may be ensuring that those who manage critical infrastructure like power plants or financial markets have access to more powerful AI than the average script kiddie (or AI writer).

Using AI that lacks regular guardrails is both thrilling and alarming. But if a cyber-reckoning is coming, then it’s probably time to tool up.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Folding iPhone
entries.summary: The iPhone with a folding screen is the first radical redesign of Apple’s flagship handset in years. The iPhone Duo will cost $1,999 when it arrives in October.
entries.content:
The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first folding smartphone. The company announced the device at its annual September event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California.

The iPhone Duo comes in Star White and Night Sky, and costs $1,999 for 256 GB of storage. While preorders kick off on October 16, the device won’t officially go on sale until October 23.

It arrives alongside the pro versions of Apple’s handsets, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.

The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, and when you open the Duo up, it reveals a second, 7.6-inch display—remarkably close to the iPad Mini’s screen size. Apple says it kept the aspect ratio consistent across both the front and inner screen for the highest quality when viewing content.

The Duo has a titanium frame with a mirror finish, Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass on the back, and Ceramic Shield 2 glass on the front. It even sports an IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating, beating Samsung to the punch. (Right now, Google's folding Pixels are the only phones with an IP68 rating.

Apple says the hinge has a “custom variable torque profile” that precisely opens and closes the phone in an “effortlessly smooth” way. When it’s open, Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. As Samsung does with its “Flex Titanium” technology, Apple uses a carbon fiber metal plate below the display to better control the stress caused by bending the display. That, alongside a nano-texture finish, helps keep the display flat and “minimizes crease visibility.” An Apple-designed scratch-resistance coating sits on top.

Surprisingly, there is no Face ID sensor, likely to save space inside the phone for the folding components. Instead, like some of Apple’s tablets, the iPhone Duo brings back the fingerprint-sensing Touch ID integrated into the side power button. This is also the first iPhone to support the USB-C Apple Pencil later this year, though there’s no way to naturally store the stylus on the edges of the device like the iPad’s magnetic Pencil dock.

Apple says the Duo has the biggest battery ever in an iPhone. Like most book-style folds, it’s a split system where a battery rests on both sides. That will net you up to 31 hours of video playback with the inner display and 44 hours with the outer display—or 24 hours of mixed overall use per charge. It also sports Apple’s new custom C2 modem (with mmWave 5G support in the US) and the A20 Pro, the same chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

There are only two cameras on the back—a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide. The lack of a telephoto zoom option is a sacrifice even Samsung made on its latest Galaxy Z Fold8. Like most book-like folds, it has two selfie cameras—a 12-megapixel camera on the outer screen and a second “FaceTime camera" on the inner display, though this one is hidden under the display.

There are familiar folding phone features here with the camera, like distracting a kid with a fun cartoon character on the outer screen to get them to look at the camera. Or your subject can preview the photo before you hit capture. The iPhone Duo can stand upright by itself, so you can set it down and it will automatically capture group photos if everyone stands at the ready.

Hardware is just one part of the story, though. The software needs to adapt and take advantage of the larger screen. Apple has been improving how apps adapt to different screen sizes for some time, making it easy for developers to scale apps from the iPhone to the iPad to the Mac, and even visionOS on the Apple Vision Pro. That means you’ll be able to enjoy iPad-like apps when unfolding the iPhone Duo.

Apple says it has moved essential controls to the side, stacked vertically, to maximize screen space. Even the dock is oriented vertically. The software transitions gracefully as you open the phone; apps will show more information—like your inbox and messages—and you can split-screen apps. You can fold it in half and set it down, and the screen will react accordingly.

Folding Time

Apple is a late entrant to the foldable phone market, which has been around since Samsung debuted the first Galaxy Fold in 2019. Since then, phone makers like Honor, Google, Motorola, and Oppo have all made folding phones. In recent years, devices have rapidly gotten slimmer, lighter, and more durable.

The iPhone Duo has a book-like shape and is similar in size to Samsung’s recent Galaxy Z Fold8, reminiscent of Google’s original Pixel Fold. This “passport-style” fold—which stands shorter and unfolds wider than many of the first wave of foldable designs—is better suited for media consumption since it eliminates the severe letterboxing that places thick black bars around the TV show or movie you’re watching.

Apple is expected to help grow a category that has been declining for five straight quarters by 13 percent year over year—potentially capturing up to 30 percent of the foldable market share by the end of 2026, according to IDC’s Nabila Popal, a senior research director. But the folding phone market is still niche, “around 2 percent by the end of this year of the global smartphone market.”

Popal says a recent IDC survey asked consumers whether they were interested in buying a foldable smartphone when it was time to upgrade, and 60 percent said they are not likely to buy one. However, when asked if Apple released a folding smartphone, almost 33 percent said they “absolutely” would.

“Apple has such a strong market pull,” Popal tells WIRED. “The average consumer didn’t know about [memory price increases] until Apple made an announcement that they’re going to increase prices. “Coming into foldables, it's going to create overall excitement for the category. And it's good for the consumer, too. It's always good to have more competition and more choice.”

One area of concern is the device’s durability and repairability, as folding phones are notoriously more prone to damage and are tough to fix. Elizabeth Chamberlain, director of Sustainability at iFixit, tells WIRED her team has never taken apart a foldable they’d call truly repairable.

“Manufacturers have come a long way since the Galaxy Fold first dropped,” she says. “But the gains in durability haven’t come with gains in repairability.”

New Economics

While Apple announced three premium iPhone models today, it is not releasing the base iPhone 18 this year—marking the first time it’s breaking up the launch cycle of the core iPhone lineup. Instead, the iPhone 18 is expected to launch in the spring of 2027 alongside the iPhone 18e and second-generation iPhone Air.

Despite the eye-watering price and the current economic climate, Popal says the iPhone Duo is “guaranteed to be a blockbuster.”

“Apple defied all odds and broke the $1,000 barrier when they first launched the $1,000 smartphone,” Popal says. “Yes, there’s going to be sticker shock, but Apple caters to a very high-end consumer segment who can afford it.”

Over the summer, Apple introduced a new iPhone leasing program to help ease the price of its phones on consumers' wallets, and it’s likely to prove popular with the uber-expensive iPhone Duo. Chamberlain says that for people who replace their phone regularly, it gives them a path to do it where the device gets back into the reuse stream and boosts the refurbished market, which isn’t a bad thing for electronic waste. However, Apple’s leasing agreements mean the device needs to be returned in the condition it was received.

“iFixit is committed to the idea that you should own your shit,” she says. “You should be able to repair things, modify things, hack your own devices. It’s sad to see the tech world move away from that principle, and Apple encouraging people to lease devices instead of buying them.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

entries.title: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Ceramic, Specs, Release Date
entries.summary: Apple’s latest smartwatches—the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4—get a faster chip, expanded health tracking, and new Siri capabilities. Plus, the ceramic finish is back.
entries.content:
Apple has unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 today during its September hardware event.

The new models retain the signature designs of their predecessors but add a faster S11 chip, new health and fitness features, and the watchOS 27 software update announced at WWDC last June.

Both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 run on the upgraded S11 chip, which Apple says delivers faster CPU and GPU performance, along with improved Siri capabilities. Apple is also expanding the smartwatch’s wellness-tracking suite with a redesigned Health app that includes a Longevity tab with new metrics, like Health Age and a Readiness score.

The health sensor array has been redesigned with more electrodes for more accurate readings, photodiodes organized in a ring to capture light more efficiently, and new LEDs that allow heart rate measurements to be collected every 5 seconds, giving you a continuous stream of heart data throughout the day.

Perhaps most notably, the Series 12 brings back the ceramic case, available in pearl white and night blue finishes. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, marketed as a luxury alternative to the company’s long-retired 18-karat gold edition; the ceramic casing was discontinued in 2020. According to Apple, the ceramic casing—made from compressed zirconia and alumina powder and polished with a diamond slurry—is four times more durable than stainless steel. The aluminum models are available in black, light gold, space gray aluminum, radiant gold, natural titanium, and a new dark bronze. All of the aluminum is recycled.

The new hardware arrives alongside watchOS 27, which will also be made available to people who already own compatible Apple Watches when the Series 12 goes on sale. The new OS updates the divisive Liquid Glass redesign on the smartwatch, and adds a more capable Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence.

Following the industry trend of AI-notetakers, the new Siri Recap can translate and transcribe real-time conversations for users. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to use their watch’s dial to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds, then read what the server said on their Apple Watch screen.

There are several features—all of them opt-in, at least for the person wearing the watch—that are powered by the watch’s ability to record the wearer’s surroundings. Read more about them in Lily Hay Newman’s story about the Apple Watch’s newfound listening abilities on WIRED.

WatchOS 27 also introduces a dynamic app grid that surfaces five Siri AI-suggested apps, the Siri app, and a shortcut to the full app grid. A new one-handed tap gesture lets you select widgets in Smart Stack, and a double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist-flick gesture can return you to the watch face, silence timers, and dismiss notifications.

Battery life remains the same for the Series 12, but the Ultra 4’s battery has expanded to up to 50 hours. A new proactive battery extension feature will notify users that tools they never use will be disabled to preserve battery life, such as gestures, Start Workout reminders, and Raise to Speak. Users can turn those abilities back on in Settings.

Like its competitors, health and fitness remain a major focus. Workout Buddy now incorporates more wellness metrics and can run without an iPhone nearby; it’s also now available in Spanish. In addition to the “Functional Strength Training” workout mode, users can now log sets, repetitions, weights, and equipment. Cycle Tracking is also gaining support for perimenopause and menopause, including notifications about cycle deviations associated with perimenopause.

With the launch of watchOS 27, Apple is removing Walkie-Talkie, its real-time voice communication tool that lets Apple Watch users communicate directly with one another.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

entries.title: You Can Now Destroy Flock Cameras for Cash in GTA V
entries.summary: A new GTA mod lets you smash and shoot Flock’s automatic license plate readers around the fictional Los Santos.
entries.content:
People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman.

The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions.

In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states.

“GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.”

In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play.

There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors.

“There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman.

Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.

GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City.

Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.”

In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice.

For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR.

“I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.”

entries.title: A Stealth Startup Thinks It Just Hacked the Memory Shortage
entries.summary: Kepler Computing claims a new approach to chip design—and a proprietary material—can help end the supply bottlenecks that have sent memory prices surging.
entries.content:
An ambitious chip startup that has spent more than seven years quietly trying to redesign the architecture for computer memory has just come out of stealth mode and believes its new approach can help ease the global memory-chip shortage—provided it can produce its technology at scale.

Kepler Computing, a San Jose, California–based startup founded in 2018 by a team of physicists and computer scientists, says it has developed a new architecture for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that directly addresses some of the chip supply bottlenecks that are constraining the computing market.

While chipmakers typically rely on expensive extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) to shrink the transistors on a chip, thereby packing more technology into the same amount of space, Kepler claims that its “3D stacking” approach and a proprietary new material allow it to increase density without relying on EUV at all—and it can work with existing semiconductor fabrication plants.

Kepler says it has made similar gains for the high-speed cache memory typically used in CPUs, GPUs, and XPUs. This so-called SRAM sits within the core of a chip die in order to cut down on data transfer times. HBM, by contrast, uses stacks of DRAM, which is a separate memory component of chips.

The company has raised $468 million in funding over the past few years from big-name backers. This includes GlobalFoundries, Intel Capital, AMD Ventures, the British investment fund Baillie Gifford, and Bill Gates, through his private Gates Frontier fund. In July, the US Department of Commerce committed to give Kepler up to $245 million to “develop in the US a new class of high-performance AI memory technology, enabled by innovative 3D and ferroelectric technologies.”

For now, much of Kepler’s testing is happening in Singapore, which is where GlobalFoundries—a manufacturing partner and investor of $50 million—has a facility. Over the past two years Kepler has been building out what it refers to as “mini fabs,” where it produces its memory chips in conjunction with Global Foundries’ 28-nanometer chips. (It has also been running tests in GlobalFoundries’ facilities in Burlington, Vermont.)

Kepler and its investors say the startup’s new approach to building memory chips couldn’t come at a better time. The global memory chip shortage has reaffirmed at least two realities about the market: Building new fabs is hugely expensive and painstaking, and the demands around certain kinds of memory tend to be cyclical. In a data-center-driven, AI-crazed world, HBM has become the memory du jour.

Some of the world’s leading memory makers, including SK Hynix and Micron, have been racing to build multibillion-dollar fabs in order to meet demand, wagering that even by the time those facilities are operational, the industry will still be looking for high-bandwidth memory.

“For a long time our thinking was that we’d work on SRAM first and then follow up with DRAM and HBM,” says Debo Olaosebikan, a Kepler Computing cofounder and its chief executive officer. “But with the launch of ChatGPT [in 2022] and the explosion of demand for an HBM alternative, we started working on our HBM road map. Now we’re making SRAM and HBM in parallel.”

“We didn’t go in thinking that this would be a replacement for DRAM or a replacement for SRAM,” says Srini Ananth, managing director at Intel Capital. “We figured the market would dictate that, and now you’re seeing a demand for both.”

In bypassing ultraviolet lithography, Kepler is one of a few tech startups working to avoid one of the major bottlenecks in semiconductor manufacturing. The startup claims it can produce SRAM that achieves the same density as 2-nanometer or 3-nanometer chips without having to invest in EUV.

“Kepler’s approach is at the sweet spot of our strategy,” says Ed Kaste, senior vice president of GlobalFoundries’ CMOS business. “It’s a new materials system, with multigenerational scaling potential, without having to build entirely new systems in the fab or invest in very expensive lithography equipment.”

Material Impact

Kepler’s overarching pitch is that the accelerated computing market shouldn’t have to wait for brand-new memory fabs to be built in order to meet demand. Instead, new approaches to building memory within existing fabs can increase supply.

Their approach is twofold. In terms of improving HBM, Kepler says it has developed a novel 3D-manufacturing technique that fits more memory chips within a fixed footprint. The core compute can then sit closer to the memory, so the data travel between the two uses less energy. Their ultimate goal is to move data around in HBM with the amount of energy that’s comparable to SRAM, all while keeping HBM’s large capacity.

Kepler also says it has improved the density of SRAM using ferroelectrics, which can read and write data at lower voltages than the mechanisms typically used to process and store data in semiconductors. The startup did this by developing a new, low-voltage, composite material that works with this ferroelectric approach.

Sasi Manipatruni, a Kepler cofounder and its chief technology officer, says the Kepler team went through 35 iterations of composites before they landed on a material class that they thought would make memory chips easier and cheaper to make.

“Once we found a way to solve the physics problem—as in the physical limitations for HBM—we came up with a material innovation that helps with the amount of memory you can have between chips,” he says.

In its early build-outs with GlobalFoundries, Kepler says it was able to convert a fab into a “next-generation” fab in just eight months, compared to a typical 24-month timeframe.

“Out goal is to take the fabs and architectures already built, and push them to the limits of physics,” Olaosebikan says.

Basically Kepler is betting that any additional costs that come from new materials or retooling existing fabs would far outweigh the $20 billion to $40 billion it costs to build new ones and outfit them with equipment worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

Waiting to Scale

Kepler Computing still has a long road ahead before it reaches full-scale production—assuming it gets there. To date, the company has run its technology on around 2,000 wafers. The startup says it’s planning to ship its first samples of HBM chips later this year, ramp up production out of Singapore next year, and start chip production in the US in 2028.

Kaste, the GlobalFoundries executive, says he’s confident that the “fundamental breakthroughs have happened. What remains is getting good results on thousands of wafers and millions of devices.”

He points out that one of the challenges with a material system like the one Kepler is using is that it includes iron in its composite. “Iron is a tough contaminant to introduce into a production facility. So Kepler’s solution has to run on dedicated equipment, or be fully encapsulated so that it can’t escape,” he says.

“The art is in keeping that material really well isolated through our production flow,” Kaste says.

Olaosebikan wouldn’t confirm the specific elements of the company’s composite material. “What I can say is, we’re using a small number of materials, and some of them aren’t what you’d typically find in mainstream ferroelectrics,” he says.

Kepler Computing isn’t the only startup looking to upend the semiconductor industry. Late last year, a well-funded startup called Substrate also made waves for its new approach to lithography, which uses nanoparticles to etch details onto advanced chips. Some industry analysts were skeptical of the startup’s ambitions, noting that it would be extremely difficult for Substrate to produce a large number of chips “that meet incredibly stringent specifications, on time and on budget,” as reported in Bloomberg.

Scale is a common challenge when attempting to innovate semiconductor manufacturing, whether with new processes, materials, or some combination of both. “The question is how to overcome all the limitations of contamination, different materials, and different tooling, in such a way that the resulting innovation can be used at scale and is worth the cost,” says Austin Lyons, a chip analyst for Creative Strategies, who was not briefed on Kepler’s innovation.

Proving out a new method for memory is one thing; meeting the historic demand for it will be another altogether.

entries.title: Apple Event Live Blog: Folding iPhone, Apple Watch Series 12, AirPods, and More
entries.summary: Get all the news when it happens, as our reporters bring you live updates from Apple Park, the company’s headquarters in Cupertino, California.
entries.content:
Get all the iPhone news as it happens. We’re reporting live from Apple Park, the company’s headquarters in Cupertino, California.

Welcome to our live coverage of today's Apple media showcase. Our reporters on the scene at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, to bring you live coverage. You'll be hearing from Julian Chokkattu, Boutayna Chokrane, Lauren Goode, Reece Rogers, and Michael Calore throughout the event.

More About How the Apple Watch Listens to You

The new Apple Watches include several “intelligent” listening features that have privacy and security baked in. But the protections can’t change the facts of what the tools do.

Read the full story about the new listening features on WIRED.

OK, so, the Duo starts at $1999. That's eye-watering, but not surprising. This is a theme across Apple's product line now, as Julian noted: Some products, like iPad and MacBook, are just more expensive.

That's partly because of bill of materials (memory), partly because Apple has not actually diversified its cash flow all that much over the past decade or so aside from growing its services business (which generates a lot of gross profit). But even as some product shipments decline—depending on which quarter you're looking at—Apple needs to maintain its margins.

Everything about the Duo is bigger, faster, longer thank other iPhones. Which is normal for Apple when it’s telling you about its new products; everything is the best version yet!

But it feels like going to a dual screen lets Apple take a significantly bigger step forward. The battery, the screen, the chips—there’s more room for all of it, and the company is really able to flex its technical muscle here.

entries.title: MS NOW Wants to Turn Its Viewers Into a Fandom
entries.summary: The cable news network’s president, Rebecca Kutler, wants to leverage its massive online and TV audience to create a fan community. First up: letting you chat with Rachel Maddow.
entries.content:
Even if you’re a casual consumer of MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, you know the names: anchors like Chris Hayes, Stephanie Ruhle, and yes, the one and only Rachel Maddow. The network has built a stable of talent who’ve amassed a massive number of casual viewers, plenty of fans … and more than a few obsessives.

Now, the network’s president, Rebecca Kutler, is looking to build that entire audience into something more akin to a fandom—turning casual viewers and fanatics alike, whether on TV or online, into paying members of an MS NOW media universe.

To do it, she’s launching an ambitious subscription program, called the MS NOW Membership, designed to connect MS NOW consumers much more directly to the Hayeses and Maddows of the world. Sure, plenty of news providers now offer subscriptions, WIRED included (and by the way, you can subscribe here). But what struck me about Kutler and Co.’s efforts was both their methodical approach—they surveyed 18,000 people before landing on a final offering—and their resolute focus on MS NOW’s deep bench of talent as the locus of their paid program. In a world where influencers are the new newscasters, and linear TV is in an inevitable decline, MS NOW is diving directly into the breach: applying the influencer playbook to build a sustainable business that’s future-proofed … at least until the next great audience pivot.

I caught up with Kutler at WIRED’s New York studios, just days before MS NOW’s subscription launch. We talked about turning TV talent into fandom magnets, beating Fox, and whether media consolidation is actually good news for the network.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Rebecca, thank you so much for being here today. Start by telling me when you joined MSNBC. What’s the timeline?

REBECCA KUTLER: I think it was right before the midterms in 2022. I had grown up at CNN. I spent more than 20 years there. I left earlier in 2022, and some folks that I knew and really respected reached out from then MSNBC, and they talked about one of those jobs that has a lot of running room and is a little ambiguous, but in the best way. I thought, “Yeah, let's check it out.” I started at MSNBC, now MS NOW, running their digital businesses, basically all their nonlinear businesses.

It gave me a real opportunity to learn the place, but also think about what are the missed opportunities that we could take advantage of in the next few years.

At some point in your tenure, you took on the whole thing.

Yes.

What were those big challenges that you identified when you looked at the whole portfolio and thought to yourself, “What are we going to do here?”

One of the things that immediately struck me when I came over was the fandom.

I had worked in other newsrooms. I have friends who work in other newsrooms. I love the news and love what we do, but I had never worked at a place where the audience really sees themselves as fans, with a deep connection to talent.

When I joined MS, it was also at the same time Jen Psaki joined, and we had known each other a little from a previous life. So we went out into the field together and did a few pretty straightforward field reporting pieces. And I've walked through airports over my career with a lot of different anchors and newspeople, but I’ve never had the experience of walking through with Jen and seeing the [attention she got]. That's why she was a great fit for MS. She’s someone people were behind and were rooting for, and had a deep connection with.

When you think about Rachel Maddow and how she lands. You’re very close to this industry. If you talk to anyone in publishing and ask them where they would ideally like to debut their book, I think most of them would say The Rachel Maddow Show. There’s a reason for that: The audience loyalty and engagement with Rachel has been proven over decades.

It’s funny, when she shares a WIRED story on social media, the traffic to that story and the engagement on her social media around WIRED is crazy. I can tell you firsthand looking at the analytics, you can feel it.

I want to ask you more about talent in a minute, but that brings me to this Membership program you're launching. I'm going to read from the press release, which I very rarely do. You will offer “new opportunities for members to interact directly with the brand’s trusted journalists, exclusive community features to engage with each other, a new roster of contributors and experts, original creator content, new verticals that explore how news and politics impacts everyday life, and 24/7 access to livestreams and television programming.”

In layman’s terms, if someone’s a MS NOW viewer, they watch it on TV sometimes, they see it on social media, what should they expect from this? What are they getting that they’re not already getting by having cable TV?

I want to answer your question directly, but I just don’t want to assume your audience is the MS NOW audience. So if you'll allow me 30 seconds …

Give us your best pitch.

We launched as a new brand about a year ago. People traditionally see us as this cable channel, and that's great. We have a huge cable audience. We're actually right now the number two most-watched basic cable channel.

Who's number one?

Fox.

I see. OK. We might talk more about that later.

But that’s just one piece of our business. We have, right now, a digital business before we even launch what we're launching this week, that has more uniques than places like Axios, Politico, The Atlantic. People spend more time with us digitally than places like the Washington Post and NPR.

And on YouTube, we have been quite efficient at building out our presence in that space. We get more clicks on YouTube than ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News combined.

I say all of that to say we are starting from a position of strength. What we are excited about, and why we're launching this product, is all those digital things I just mentioned, we don't have a way to catch all those people if they’re not going to be watching cable.

Got it.

It’s taking our current superfans who watch us on linear and giving them more. So what are they going to get? They're going to get direct access to our talent. Seven days a week at noon and at 6:00 pm, if you are a member of the MS NOW community, you can hop on and directly interact with one of our anchors or one of our reporters.

On Monday it’s going to be Rachel Maddow, and then you go through the week. You're going to hear from Michael Steele, you’re going to hear from Jen Psaki, you're going to hear from Reverend Al Sharpton. You’re going to hear from the people that you know and love from watching them on MS NOW and have the opportunity to ask them your question directly, and not just interact with our talent, but also interact with each other.

When we started this process around a year and a half ago, we didn’t just sit in a conference room and think, “Hmm, let’s make another commodity news app.” Because let's be honest, a lot of that already exists. What we did was actually start from a place of product research. We went out to 18,000 people. We did surveys, we did in-person interviews, and we spent time taking that research and getting to where we are this week.

What I most want people to know is, what you see this week will look vastly different six months from now and a year from now if we're doing our jobs right. What we need to do is build and learn and test and add investment and expand where we need to, but not really think that we’re going to get it all right on day one, but give ourselves that latitude.

Is the goal to pull linear viewers onto digital, or is it to better engage the digital audience, or both?

It's both. All those people consuming us on YouTube, on digital, on social, in audio, 90 percent of those people do not regularly consume us on linear television. So a big function of this product is to say, “Hey, you’re watching YouTube videos all the time of Lawrence O'Donnell. Maybe you’re not someone who's going to be a cable subscriber. But can you come join our community in another capacity? Can we create a product that entices you to be part of an MS NOW community, even if you're someone who's reluctant to become a cable customer?”

I would say that, for the average person, if you ask them, “Fox News, MS NOW, who do those networks reach?” I would say Fox News reaches Republicans, and that’s who has it on TV, that's who’s going to that website. I would say MS NOW reaches progressives, Democrats, left-leaning people. Is that a stated goal for you, or do you want that tent to be bigger?

Is the audience for MS NOW different from the audience for Fox? Of course it is. There's probably a small amount of overlap, but not a lot, and that's OK.

For example, when I think forward to election night, I gotta say, I think there’s nowhere I'd rather hang out on election night than at our table with Rachel and Nicolle [Wallace] and Lawrence and Chris [Hayes] and Michael [Steele] and everyone.

What we try to do is be smart, respect our audience, and be a fun place, and a place where, again, Michael Steele is a big part of our election night. He was chairman of the Republican National Committee.

Right.

We have a broad range of views, but I think they all fall under that pro-democracy banner.

Are you competitive? Do you want to beat Fox? Do you want to see that number one?

Look, I am a pretty competitive person. I just see who our competition is as wider than that typical cable landscape.

I want to build a great product right now and have a large membership community, and I want to make sure that we are competing on every battleground.

That is yes, absolutely on cable, yes on digital, yes on YouTube, yes in audio. I think that because of the life that this brand lived under previous ownership, there were times when our wings were clipped a little from a business perspective, and that wasn't—if I was sitting in the seats of the leadership team at NBC, I might have made the same decisions.

When you’re working for the very large, very successful companies that NBCUniversal and Comcast are, they need to look at the whole company and figure out where best to invest their dollars. So what they did makes sense for them. But now we're lucky to be a part of Versant, and Versant has several pieces of their portfolio that generate a lot of cash.

What is Versant, for those who may not know?

Versant is the spinoff, so a spinout, of NBCUniversal. For folks that weren't following along day by day, around a year ago, NBCUniversal spun out a series of businesses. Those include what is now MS NOW, CNBC, brands like E!—you know, Live from the Red Carpet—and then golf.

We are now part of a company that is incentivized to invest the money that we earn as MS NOW back into MS NOW. We're just no longer part of a company that has to invest in theme parks and other things that, for that company, made a lot of sense.

I don’t think it’s a secret that cable news audiences are declining, and I’m going to ask this in the bluntest possible way: That’s an older audience, so what do you do when they die?

I am not blind to the long-term challenges. That’s why we are investing in digital. But do I think the cable business right now for MS NOW is quite healthy? I do.

Our average viewer watches nine hours a week.

That is a lot of MS NOW.

Do I wake up in a panic in the middle of the night? No. Do I know there are long-term challenges? Yes.

What do you wake up at night worrying about? Working in media and journalism is hard. It's a hard business, and these are really difficult transformations to try to undertake, and to undertake successfully. What's the hardest part of this for you right now?

What I wake up angsty about sometimes is I know we have this guest or that guest coming up, but how can we upgrade? How can we make it better? What is the better question? What is the better way in?

I might be old-school when I say this, but I think content always wins. Every single race.

I want to ask more about talent. You do have some real fandom magnets. I think one of the biggest challenges in publishing today, especially on digital, is that it is so noisy. There is so much competition. It’s not just news, but it’s everything on someone's Instagram feed. How do you encourage your journalists, your talent, to break through that in a digital context?

I'll just pick on Chris Hayes for a minute here. Because there’s almost no time that I talk to Chris Hayes that I don’t then hang up the phone or walk out of his office and think to myself, “That guy’s brain is huge.”

I think that’s the answer to the question of how do you break through? Every brand and every place in the media has to figure out what their breakthrough is. Look, there's people who want to break through by showing cat videos all day. People want to break through by writing outrageous headlines that aren’t really based in facts.

Yes.

Where I want MS NOW to break through is being brainiacs, is coming to the table with something that is intellectually interesting, that is showing me something or teaching me something or adding value to a news story in a way I hadn’t thought about it before, of drawing on their experience, decades of experience working in the room, being in the room where it happened.

What has the experience been like of transitioning some of the more TV-comfortable talent that you have, who are accustomed to doing a cable news show, and saying to them, “Now you do these interactive sessions with our audience, now you do TikTok, now you participate in these other parts of the ecosystem”?

One of my rules is: don’t do anything that feels weird for you. What I mean by that is, if you in your own life don’t use TikTok, I don’t recommend trying to become a TikToker. It’s going to land weird. We’ve seen it. So what I have encouraged our shows, our hosts, everyone in the MS NOW family, to do is don’t try to be everywhere. Don’t try to be everything.

I mean, a great example, Symone Sanders [Townsend] is fantastic at TikTok and Instagram because she grew up in those spaces and knows those audiences. That might not be the same for Lawrence O’Donnell. Lawrence O’Donnell is a huge hit on YouTube.

What has Trump 2.0 been like over there? Have you seen an audience bump? Have you seen fatigue? The challenge with the story of Trump 2.0 is that there are a thousand stories a day. How are you thinking about reaching your audience in a way that can grab them and hold them?

What I want our audience to know is that we are who we are, and we’re proud of who we are, and you can come to us on any platform at any time and trust that you are getting our best reporting and our best analysis without fear.

We haven’t talked about it yet, but as part of the spinoff, we had to build our own newsroom. What we tried to do is build our newsroom knowing the moment. We’re not trying to be commodity news. We’re trying to build an absolutely kickass DC newsroom, and I think we’ve done that.

MS NOW is one of the very few media brands in growth mode right now. It's impressive.

I'm curious about your take on the possibility of a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which would place CNN and CBS News under one owner. Would that consolidation be good for you? Does this help you even if the broader implications can be troubling?

In a functioning healthy democracy, you need a very healthy free and fair press. So I am rooting for better, stronger newsrooms. I worked most of my career at CNN, and while they might be technically a competitor or rival now, the world is a better place with a stronger CNN.
